column14: No funding, acknowledgement or competing-interest statement appears in the manuscript. Work is industry-affiliated (Microsoft Research / Microsoft) in collaboration with MIT. Footnote 1 states the chapter expands the authors' Harvard Business Review article [3].
column17: The chapter describes a designed artefact - an LLM-based interaction layer over existing supply chain planning/optimization tools, with an explicit data flow (question handler, LLM, application code, supply chain tool/data repository, interpreter; Fig. 1, p. 4) - and reports its instantiation and production deployment in Microsoft's cloud supply chain (Section 6). BORDERLINE: the chapter has no methodology section, no stated research design and no primary data collection; the technical design is credited to prior work ([1] Li et al. 2023) and the chapter is a thought-leadership contribution to an edited volume that 'expands' an HBR article (footnote 1, p. 1). 'conceptual' is therefore defensible; coded 'design-science' because an artefact is specified and evaluated rather than merely envisioned. R1 decision needed.
column19: A working system exists and is in production: 'The LLM-based technology was tested extensively in research and product teams before it was shipped in production' (p. 7); it serves Microsoft cloud supply chain planners via a user-facing portal with a demand drift analyzer and a fulfillment-plan Q&A system (p. 8). Quantitative outcomes are reported (~90% answer accuracy; ~23% saving of fulfillment investigation time; cycle times of minutes vs. about a week). BORDERLINE: the evaluation is reported only in aggregate - no test-set size, no accuracy definition, no per-model results, no baseline system, no ablation, no statistical treatment, and the 23% figure is explicitly an estimate; 'prototype' could be argued on reporting grounds. Coded 'implemented-validated' because the system is in production use with quantitative figures. R1 decision needed.
column20: Primary: cloud computing / hyperscale datacenter hardware supply chain (Microsoft Azure - 'tens of regions worldwide and hundreds of datacenters', p. 6). Secondary examples: chemical manufacturing procurement and automotive OEM procurement (Section 7, pp. 8-9); a synthetic discrete-manufacturing scenario (raw-material suppliers, factories, retailers) used in testing (p. 7).
column21: Microsoft cloud supply chain (Section 6). Example 1: monthly demand drift analysis - LLM ingests the cloud hardware demand plan from different periods and auto-generates an email report of all changes, the person who made each change, the input that led to it, the root cause (e.g. a new, more efficient hardware generation needing fewer servers) and potential errors for planner review. Example 2: Q&A over the fulfillment plan produced by optimization tools (hardware supplier choice, cluster dock date, deployment location - selection of a row of tiles), answering what-if questions such as the cost increase of docking a demand a week earlier or deactivating a warehouse for one week. Section 7: contract template redesign at a large chemical manufacturer and contract-discount compliance analysis at an automotive OEM.
column22: NR - no research questions are stated. Stated purpose: 'we report how this disruptive technology can democratize supply chain technology - namely, facilitate the understanding of tools' outcomes, as well as the interaction with supply chain tools without human-in-the-loop' (Abstract, p. 1), addressing three challenges: (i) understanding and explaining tool recommendations, (ii) analyzing scenarios / answering what-if questions, (iii) updating the mathematical models to reflect current business environments. Section 1: 'the goal of applying LLM technology for supply chains is to automate key decision-making processes, without compromising the quality of the decisions' (p. 2).
column24: Mapped to 'SC-network-design' on the strength of the paper's own application list: the LLM technology is applied 'for reasoning about supply chain data and tools used for Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP), Network Strategy, Supply Chain Resiliency and Inventory Optimization' (p. 2), and Section 1 names 'network design' among the tool classes addressed. BOUNDARY CASE: the two deployed cases reported in depth (demand drift analysis; fulfillment-plan Q&A on supplier choice, dock dates and cluster placement) are tactical/executional rather than network-configuring, and the procurement examples (Section 7) are contract management. No site selection, technology selection, factory planning or GPN content. If R1 requires a strategic subdomain to be evidenced by a reported case rather than by the paper's framing, this study is out of scope or should be flagged for exclusion; alternatively 'logistics-distribution-network-design' could be added on the basis of the 'add a new transit lane between two locations' recommendation module (p. 8). Escalation recommended.
column26: The activities the LLM actually performs are not covered by the controlled vocabulary: (a) natural-language data discovery and explanation of optimization-tool recommendations (Section 3); (b) what-if / scenario analysis by translating a user question into 'mathematical code' that applies a small change (e.g. an added constraint) to the existing mathematical model, re-solving and verbalising the comparison (Section 4); (c) interactive re-planning / model updating after disruptions, e.g. regenerating an S&OP plan that avoids a facility down for seven days (Section 5); (d) demand-plan drift analysis with root-cause attribution (Section 6); (e) procurement contract template generation and contract-compliance analysis (Section 7). 'SC-network-configuration' and 'capacity-dimensioning' are coded for the underlying domain tools the LLM interfaces with (network design/network strategy; cloud hardware deployment against a demand plan) - both are mentioned rather than demonstrated as LLM tasks, so R1 may prefer 'other' alone.
column29: A horizon is stated, but a tactical one: 'the demand is exposed through a demand plan, which summarizes important information about demand requests for the next year or so' (p. 6), i.e. an annual rolling plan monitored monthly ('Planners and executives monitor the changes in the demand plan ... monthly', p. 6); other temporal references are shorter still (a facility 'down for seven days', docking 'a week earlier', deactivating a warehouse 'for one week'). Strategic reading: the chapter positions the technology over 'Network Strategy' and 'network design' tools (p. 2) and over cloud hardware deployment decisions that avoid 'over-provisioning of hardware' (p. 6), i.e. capital-intensive capacity commitments. Upper-tactical/operational reading: every reported deployment operates on a within-year plan and on execution-level what-if questions. Coded 'ambiguous' with a lean towards upper-tactical; R1 decision needed, including on scope eligibility.
column31: Not framed as system-configuring by the authors. The reported decisions execute a given demand plan rather than determine what exists: the fulfillment plan assigns and ships servers from warehouses to datacenters, choosing '(i) the hardware supplier that will be used to fulfill the demand, (ii) the timeline of the deployment - in particular, the cluster's dock-date, and (iii) the particular cluster's deployment location in the data center (selection of a row of tiles)' (p. 7). AMBIGUITY: on the substance, installing clusters in datacenters does set the installed capacity of the cloud ('cloud providers periodically make hardware deployment decisions ... while avoiding over-provisioning of hardware', p. 6), so a substance-based reading could code TRUE; coded FALSE because the paper frames this as fulfillment of an externally given demand plan and because the LLM's role is explanation and what-if analysis, not the configuring decision itself.
column34: An LLM-based interaction layer placed between planners and existing supply chain planning tools, with three functions. (1) Data discovery and insights: the LLM translates plain-language questions ('How much raw material of type T does supplier S have today?', 'Which was the most productive factory last week?') into data science queries executed against the company's data repository (e.g. a SQL database), and verbalises the numeric result; proprietary data need not be sent to the LLM service, which the authors highlight as a privacy advantage (Section 3, p. 3). (2) What-if answering: the LLM translates the human query into 'mathematical code' - a small change to the original mathematical program used to produce the plan, e.g. adding a constraint that prohibits factories other than F from shipping to retailer R - which is fed to the supply chain tool to produce a modified plan used only for comparison with the incumbent; the LLM then renders the comparison in natural language (Section 4, pp. 3-5). The design principle is explicit: 'not to replace the mathematical model with LLMs but rather use the mathematical model in tandem with LLMs' (p. 4). (3) Interactive planning: planners ask the technology to update the model and re-plan (e.g. generate a new S&OP plan avoiding a facility down for seven days, reporting the updated plan, new cost, demand lost and profitability impact), and the technology can itself raise alarms (e.g. detecting supplier lead-time drift from historical shipment data, predicting arrival and proposing corrective action) (Section 5, p. 5). Data flow (Fig. 1, p. 4): user question -> question handler, which appends question/answer example pairs from a large curated repository -> LLM (in-context learning) -> application code -> supply chain tool (e.g. optimization solver) and/or the application's data repository -> application output -> interpreter -> LLM -> plain-language answer to the user. Deployed instantiations at Microsoft: a demand drift analyzer that ingests demand plans from different periods and emits an email report of changes, change owners, root causes and potential errors for planner review; a fulfillment-plan Q&A system for what-if questions; and, more recently, insight and recommendation modules integrated into the fulfillment systems (e.g. recommending a new transit lane between two locations) (Section 6, pp. 6-8). Inputs: natural-language planner queries plus company plan/transaction data and the existing optimization model; outputs: natural-language answers, explanations, root-cause reports, comparative modified plans and recommendations.

column36: 'Multiple language models and training approaches have been tested, including in-context learning for the larger models such as GPT-4 (OpenAI), and fine-tuning for smaller open-sourced models such as Llama-2 from Meta and Phi-2 from Microsoft. The current deployment uses GPT-4 and achieves around 90% accuracy' (p. 7). GPT-4 therefore performs all production roles (query-to-code translation and output interpretation); Llama-2 and Phi-2 appear only in pre-deployment testing, with no results reported for them. Model versions/dates, context lengths, temperature and other decoding parameters are not reported. Small Language Models are discussed as a future cost-reduction option ([5], Section 8, p. 10).
column38: Phi (Phi-2, Microsoft small language model), tested but not deployed.
column40: The deployed model, GPT-4 (OpenAI), is proprietary. The models tested alongside it are explicitly characterised as open: 'fine-tuning for smaller open-sourced models such as Llama-2 from Meta and Phi-2 from Microsoft' (p. 7), and the research team 'is actively examining different open-source models'. Coded 'mixed' on the full set of models reported; if R1 scopes the field to the deployed system only, 'N' applies.
column42: The deployed system performs no weight updates: adaptation is by in-context learning, feeding the LLM (prompt, answer) example pairs drawn from 'a large repository of questions and code answers' appended to the user query by the question handler (Sections 2 and 4, pp. 3-5); 'A key advantage of this approach is that the LLM can be used as-is, without requiring any parameter tuning' (p. 3). Fine-tuning was applied only to the smaller open-source candidates (Llama-2, Phi-2) during pre-deployment testing (p. 7), with no method (full, LoRA, other), data volume or results reported, and is discussed in Section 8 as one costly option among alternatives (RAG, SLMs). Prompt texts and the example repository are not published. AMBIGUITY: because fine-tuning was actually performed on tested models, R1 could code 'other' with the specification 'unspecified fine-tuning of Llama-2 and Phi-2 during model selection; deployed configuration uses in-context learning only'.
column50: NR - referred to generically as 'optimization solvers' and 'supply chain tool'; no solver product named. Background on the Microsoft fulfillment optimization is deferred to [2] (Liu et al., M&SOM 2025).
column51: The optimization model is the substrate the LLM operates on, not something the LLM replaces: 'supply chain planning tools use mathematical models, typically optimization methods, to generate a recommendation ... many optimization tasks are written in the form of mathematical programs, which transfer the structure of the supply chain and all the business requirements into a mathematical model. A key idea behind our design is not to replace the mathematical model with LLMs but rather use the mathematical model in tandem with LLMs' (p. 4). The LLM emits small model edits, e.g. 'adding a mathematical requirement (referred to as constraint) that prohibits other factories from sending products to that retailer' (p. 4), and the modified model is re-solved for comparison. Concrete formulation (Microsoft cloud fulfillment, Section 6, p. 7): decision variables = hardware supplier per demand request, deployment timeline / cluster dock-date, and cluster placement location (row of tiles) in the datacenter; objective = 'minimize the total cost that consists of multiple components, such as shipping costs and delay cost of the clusters compared to their ideal dock-date'; constraints = compatibility, capacity, inventory, operational throughputs. 'mature-MILP' is coded because these are large-scale, solver-based mathematical programs with linear cost structure and discrete assignment decisions ([2]); NOTE: the paper never names the model class (MILP is not stated), so this is an inference from the described formulation - R1 should verify against [2].

column87: ["End-to-end model generation is not yet viable: the technology is 'currently capable of modeling simple supply chain structures but is not capable today of reliably modeling a more complex, industrial, environment', and no tools exist to validate a complete LLM-generated mathematical model or to identify what is missing and how to correct it (Section 5, p. 5).", "Verifying correctness of LLM output, especially generated code, is an open challenge, including whether a generated formulation can be solved in reasonable time; the authors expect LLMs to occasionally produce wrong outputs, so designers must invest in identifying mistakes and recovering from them (Section 8, p. 10).", "Question ambiguity: optimization is a precise 'language' while user phrasing is not (the example 'Can we utilize factory F better?' admits several objectives), so users must be trained to ask precise questions or the framework must generate clarifying questions until the query is unequivocal (Section 8, pp. 9-10).", "Data availability and quality: decision making requires clean, reliable data; missing or inconsistent data can render planning tools obsolete, and keeping proprietary data out of the LLM framework may not be fully possible when user-specific data must be added to the query for context (Section 8, p. 10).", "Cost and performance trade-offs are unresolved: fine-tuning is costly, while appending domain data via RAG lengthens the query and raises cost per query (Section 8, p. 10).", "Coverage is deliberately limited: a gradual deployment strategy means the technology currently supports only the most common what-if questions, with coverage expanded over time as user interactions, accuracy and fallback mechanisms are monitored (Section 6, p. 7)."]
column88: The chapter reports a successful production deployment rather than a controlled study. The LLM-plus-optimization design (LLM translates queries into small edits of an existing mathematical program, solver re-solves, LLM verbalises the comparison) was tested internally on per-scenario question sets including deliberately awkward and atypical questions, across multiple models and adaptation strategies; the shipped configuration uses GPT-4 with in-context learning and reaches around 90% accuracy. In Microsoft's cloud supply chain, demand drift analysis that previously required a week and the involvement of program managers, data scientists and engineers is now completed by planners in minutes, with root causes (e.g. a new hardware generation requiring fewer servers, or customers reducing requirements) attributed automatically and potential errors flagged for review; fulfillment-plan what-if questions are answered in minutes instead of days, with an estimated 23% saving of fulfillment investigation time and, the authors state, no loss of answer accuracy. Adoption was supported by an internal portal with AI/LLM courses and an interface that separates the drift analyzer from the Q&A system and tells planners which question types are supported. Two planner quotes attest to reduced ticket volume to engineering and changed daily practice. Insight and recommendation modules (e.g. adding a transit lane between two locations) have since been integrated into the fulfillment systems. Procurement examples report a chemical manufacturer unifying contract templates by product category and an automotive OEM recovering unclaimed volume discounts worth millions of dollars. NOTE ON EVIDENCE QUALITY: all figures are developer-reported aggregates without protocol, sample size, baseline system, ablation or independent assessment; the abstract's claim of interaction 'without human-in-the-loop' refers to removing data-scientist intermediaries, not to removing the planner, who remains the decision maker throughout.
column91: The central contribution is a scenario-analysis interface for planners: natural-language what-if questions are turned into modified mathematical models whose re-solved plan 'is used only for comparison with the existing one' (Section 4, p. 4), so the system produces comparisons for human judgement rather than executing changes. Section 5 extends this to interactive planning, where the planner asks for a re-plan around a disruption and receives the updated plan plus new cost, demand lost and profitability impact, and where the technology raises alarms (e.g. supplier lead-time drift) that the planner then acts on by requesting a re-run. Review points remain human: the drift-analysis email 'points out potential errors that planners can review and adjust' (p. 6), and planners 'confirm that it meets business needs' when receiving optimization output (p. 7). The UI supports this by separating the two tools and publishing the supported question types (p. 8). AMBIGUITY: the abstract simultaneously advertises 'interaction with supply chain tools without human-in-the-loop', which in context means without data-scientist/engineer intermediaries rather than without planner oversight - R1 should note this tension. The error-review step in the drift report could alternatively be coded 'approval-gate'; Section 8's proposal that 'the LLM framework would have to generate clarifying questions' until the question is unequivocal is future work, not an implemented escalation protocol.
column95: Two formalizations are reported, neither an ontology, knowledge graph or standard. (1) The existing mathematical program is treated as the authoritative encoding of domain knowledge: mathematical programs 'transfer the structure of the supply chain and all the business requirements into a mathematical model' (p. 4), and the LLM is confined to emitting small, verifiable edits to that model rather than reasoning about the domain itself - the paper's factuality mechanism. (2) A curated repository of (question, mathematical-code) pairs, portions of which the question handler appends to each user query for in-context learning (p. 5; details in [1]). Company data sits in a separate relational repository (e.g. SQL) queried by LLM-generated code (p. 3). AMBIGUITY: the formalization is the OR model already captured under or_substrate, so R1 may prefer FALSE (no ontology, knowledge graph or standards encoding is reported, and no schema, taxonomy or vocabulary is described).
column96: Optimization model as domain-knowledge encoding (supply chain structure and business requirements formalised as a mathematical program) plus a curated question-to-mathematical-code example repository used for in-context learning.
column99: An internally developed, explicitly named evaluation methodology: 'A general evaluation methodology has been developed to test the effectiveness of the LLM technology. In a nutshell, the methodology involves creating a set of test questions for each example. Some of the questions are challenging, for example include incorrect grammar, or atypical questions for the specific domain' (p. 7), applied across the Microsoft cases and synthetic cross-domain scenarios and scored as answer accuracy (~90% for the deployed GPT-4 configuration). Post-deployment monitoring of user interactions, accuracy and fallback mechanisms extends it into production (p. 7). Coded 'other' rather than 'benchmark' because the suite is proprietary, unpublished, not standardized and not quantified (no size, no scoring rubric, no inter-rater procedure); R1 may prefer 'benchmark' if a reusable internal test suite qualifies, or FALSE if only published frameworks count.
column100: Proprietary internal test-question suite per application scenario, including adversarial/atypical phrasings, scored as answer accuracy, plus production monitoring of accuracy and fallback rates.
column102: Score 1 - description insufficient to replicate. The chapter is a practitioner-facing account with no methodology section. Reported: the conceptual data flow (Fig. 1), the design principle of LLM-plus-mathematical-model, the adaptation strategy (in-context learning from a question/code repository), the deployed model (GPT-4) and the two Microsoft use cases. Missing: all prompts and example pairs, the repository construction procedure, the question-handler and interpreter implementation, model versions and decoding parameters, the optimization model itself, the size and content of the evaluation question sets, the definition and scoring of 'accuracy', the basis of the 23% estimate, per-model results, any code or data. Technical detail is explicitly delegated to prior publications ([1], [2]) and footnote 1 positions the chapter as an expansion of an HBR article. Replication from this text alone is not possible.
column104: Score 3 - implemented plus quantitative evaluation, under the rubric's literal wording. The system is not merely prototyped but shipped to production in a large real supply chain (Microsoft Azure), preceded by internal testing across scenarios and models, and outcomes are quantified (~90% accuracy; ~23% fulfillment investigation time saved; week-to-minutes and days-to-minutes cycle-time reductions), supplemented by user testimony and third-party procurement outcomes. CAVEAT: the quantitative evidence is thin and entirely developer-reported - two aggregate figures, one of them an estimate, with no sample sizes, no protocol, no baseline system, no ablation and no independent assessment. If R1 recodes validation_status to 'prototype' or judges that unprotocolled aggregate figures do not constitute quantitative evaluation, this dimension should drop to 2.
